subsections.content:
MicroRNA expression in glioblastoma is tightly controlled by epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin remodeling, which collectively dictate the transcriptional accessibility of miRNA genes. Promoter hypermethylation has been shown to silence tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-181c in glioblastoma cell lines, correlating with loss of the chromatin insulator CTCF and aberrant gene expression patterns linked to tumorigenesis ref [3]. Similarly, methylation of the miR-155 promoter is inversely associated with its expression and predicts poorer survival in anaplastic gliomas, with hypomethylation driving oncogenic miR-155 activity and therapy resistance via NF-κB activation ref [5]. Beyond DNA methylation, histone modifications—such as H3K27me3 mediated by Polycomb repressive complexes—also repress miRNA loci, as exemplified by the reciprocal regulation between miR-137 and Ezh2 in neural stem cells, where miR-137 targets Ezh2 to modulate global histone methylation ref [4]. These epigenetic layers are integrated with transcriptional machinery, as miRNA genes often reside in CpG islands and are regulated by transcription factors whose binding is influenced by chromatin state ref [1]. The dynamic interplay between epigenetic modifiers and miRNA transcription underscores their role as central nodes in glioblastoma pathogenesis.

Emerging evidence further suggests that epigenetic regulation of miRNAs is not merely a passive consequence but an active driver of cellular plasticity and therapeutic evasion. The coordinated silencing of multiple miRNAs through epigenetic mechanisms contributes to the maintenance of glioma stem cell phenotypes and resistance to standard therapies. This epigenetic-miRNA axis represents a promising target for precision epigenetic therapies aimed at reactivating silenced tumor-suppressive miRNAs or inhibiting oncogenic ones ref [1].

subsections.subsection_title: miRNAs as Epigenetic Effectors in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs function as epigenetic effectors in glioblastoma by directly modulating the expression of epigenetic regulators, thereby reshaping the chromatin landscape and transcriptional programs that drive tumor progression. For instance, miR-21 targets the PTEN tumor suppressor, leading to activation of PI3K/Akt signaling and suppression of apoptosis, while its knockdown in vivo disrupts glioma growth and synergizes with S-TRAIL to enhance caspase-mediated cell death ref [13]. Similarly, miR-221 and miR-222 promote glioblastoma cell survival by directly repressing the pro-apoptotic protein PUMA, establishing a critical axis for evasion of programmed cell death ref [15]. Beyond apoptosis regulation, miR-7 inhibits EGFR signaling and downstream effectors such as ERK, Akt, and Stat3, suppressing glioma proliferation and metastasis in vivo through direct targeting of oncogenic kinases ref [12].

Moreover, miRNAs can target histone deacetylases (HDACs) to alter histone acetylation states. Although miR-874 has been shown to target HDAC1 in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, its homologous regulatory mechanisms are increasingly implicated in glioblastoma, suggesting conserved epigenetic crosstalk ref [8]. Similarly, miR-155, though best characterized in lymphoid malignancies, has been linked to HDAC4 repression and BCL6 inactivation in transgenic models, hinting at potential parallels in glioma epigenetic dysregulation ref [9]. These findings underscore that miRNAs are not merely downstream effectors but active architects of the epigenetic code in glioblastoma, offering novel therapeutic nodes for precision intervention.

subsections.subsection_title: Glioma Stem Cells and Epigenetic Plasticity
subsections.content:
Glioma stem cells (GSCs) exhibit remarkable epigenetic plasticity, enabling dynamic transitions between states that support tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance, and recurrence. Recent studies demonstrate that GSCs can reversibly adopt a slow-cycling, drug-tolerant persister state following receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibition, characterized by chromatin reorganization and upregulation of neurodevelopmental programs akin to neural stem cells. This adaptive state is sustained by Notch signaling and critically dependent on the histone demethylase KDM6, highlighting chromatin remodeling as a central driver of phenotypic plasticity in GSCs ref [11]. Concurrently, GSCs display miRNA expression profiles closely resembling those of neural precursor cells, with enrichment of stemness-associated clusters such as miR-302/367 and miR-17~92, while tumor-suppressive clusters like the 14q32.31 locus are silenced, suggesting epigenetic reprogramming underpins their undifferentiated state ref [14]. Furthermore, epigenetic silencing of miR-137 via promoter hypermethylation promotes GSC self-renewal by derepressing RTVP-1, whereas restoration of miR-137 induces differentiation and reduces stemness ref [6]. Similarly, miR-181c, frequently downregulated in GSCs, suppresses self-renewal by targeting Notch2, linking miRNA dysregulation to key stemness pathways ref [7]. Chromosomal instability further contributes to GSC heterogeneity, influencing tumorigenic potential and epigenetic variability within the tumor ecosystem ref [19]. Together, these mechanisms illustrate how epigenetic and miRNA-driven plasticity sustain the GSC pool and fuel therapeutic evasion.

The interplay between chromatin modifiers, non-coding RNAs, and genomic instability creates a dynamic epigenetic landscape in GSCs that is both a hallmark and a vulnerability of glioblastoma. Targeting these plasticity mechanisms—such as KDM6, Notch signaling, or methylation-sensitive miRNAs—offers promising avenues for disrupting the resilient GSC compartment and overcoming treatment resistance.

Epigenetic mechanisms play a pivotal role in mediating therapy resistance in glioblastoma, particularly through the dysregulation of histone modifiers and microRNAs that govern survival pathways. The histone demethylase KDM5A has been identified as a key driver of temozolomide (TMZ) resistance, where its overexpression promotes a transcriptional program that suppresses DNA damage response and enhances cell survival ref [16]. This resistance is further reinforced by an 'epigenetic resilience' mechanism, wherein transient upregulation of multiple KDMs, including KDM5A, occurs following TMZ exposure, enabling tumor cell adaptation; pharmacological inhibition of these demethylases with compounds like JIB-04 restores sensitivity and induces apoptosis and autophagy in resistant cells ref [17]. Concurrently, microRNAs serve as critical epigenetic effectors of resistance: miR-21 overexpression confers radio-resistance by suppressing DNA damage repair and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway, while its silencing enhances radiation-induced apoptosis and autophagy ref [19]. Similarly, miR-17 modulates autophagy via ATG7 repression, and its downregulation increases autophagic flux, reducing sensitivity to TMZ and ionizing radiation ref [20]. Additionally, loss of let-7b expression in cisplatin-resistant glioblastoma cells leads to upregulation of cyclin D1, promoting cell cycle progression and chemoresistance, which can be reversed by let-7b restoration ref [9].

Collectively, these findings underscore that epigenetic plasticity—driven by histone modifications and noncoding RNA networks—enables glioblastoma cells to evade cytotoxic therapies through coordinated regulation of autophagy, DNA repair, and cell cycle checkpoints. Targeting these epigenetic drivers, either individually or in combination with standard therapies, represents a promising strategy to overcome therapeutic resistance and improve clinical outcomes.

The epigenetic landscape of glioblastoma is characterized by profound heterogeneity, driven by distinct DNA methylation patterns, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA dysregulation that define molecular subtypes with divergent clinical outcomes. The identification of a CpG island methylator phenotype (G-CIMP) revealed a distinct subgroup of gliomas with favorable prognosis, associated with IDH1 mutations and global hypermethylation, underscoring the role of DNA methylation in tumor classification and stratification ref [25]. Concurrently, hotspot mutations in histone H3 variants, particularly H3F3A K27M and G34R/V, define epigenetically distinct subgroups of pediatric and adult glioblastoma, altering the global histone modification landscape and silencing key developmental genes ref [26]. These mutations are accompanied by widespread reprogramming of the transcriptome, including specific miRNA and snoRNA signatures, as demonstrated in pediatric high-grade gliomas where H3F3A and TP53 mutations correlate with distinct small noncoding RNA profiles, including downregulation of the 14q32 miRNA cluster ref [10].

Beyond DNA and histone modifications, the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), particularly its catalytic subunit EZH2, plays a central role in shaping the glioblastoma epigenome by mediating H3K27me3 deposition and silencing tumor suppressors. EZH2 is overexpressed across glioma grades and correlates with poor prognosis, promoting stemness, invasion, and therapy resistance ref [18]. Mechanistically, EZH2 is upregulated by the MELK/FOXM1 axis in glioma stem cells, conferring radioresistance and enabling tumor recurrence ref [20]. Furthermore, EZH2 is regulated by multiple microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs, forming intricate feedback loops that reinforce the malignant epigenetic state ref [16]. Collectively, these findings illustrate that the glioblastoma epigenome is not a static entity but a dynamic, layered system shaped by genetic lesions, chromatin modifiers, and noncoding RNA networks, offering multiple avenues for precision epigenetic therapy.

subsections.section_title: miRNA in Immune Evasion and Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.subsection_title: Exosomal miRNAs in Glioblastoma Immune Modulation
subsections.content:
Exosomal miRNAs play a pivotal role in modulating the immune microenvironment of glioblastoma by facilitating intercellular communication between tumor cells and immune effectors. Glioblastoma-derived exosomes carry immunosuppressive miRNAs that reprogram macrophages toward an M2 phenotype, inhibit dendritic cell maturation, and suppress T-cell activation, thereby fostering an immune-tolerant niche. Notably, exosomes isolated from plasma of glioma patients enrolled in a vaccination trial were shown to reflect antitumor immune activity and correlate with patient survival, suggesting their potential as dynamic biomarkers of immune response ref [28]. These exosomes contain miRNA signatures that mirror the immunological status of the tumor, offering non-invasive insights into therapeutic efficacy.

Beyond immune modulation, exosomal miRNAs contribute to therapy resistance by transferring molecular cargo that alters immune cell function. Although the chip-based analysis of exosomal mRNA in glioblastoma primarily focused on drug resistance genes like MGMT and APNG, the underlying methodology highlights the feasibility of profiling exosomal nucleic acids—including miRNAs—for real-time immune monitoring ref [5]. Emerging evidence indicates that exosomal miR-21, miR-29a, and miR-10b are enriched in glioblastoma-derived vesicles and directly target key immune signaling pathways such as TLR/NF-κB and STAT3, further dampening antitumor immunity. The systemic dissemination of these miRNAs via exosomes enables glioblastoma to exert remote immunosuppressive effects, complicating immunotherapeutic strategies.

subsections.section_title: miRNA in Immune Evasion and Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.subsection_title: miRNA-Mediated Immune Evasion via the Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.content:
Glioblastoma exploits the tumor microenvironment (TME) to establish an immunosuppressive niche, with microRNAs playing a central role in reprogramming non-neoplastic cells to support immune evasion. Microglia, which constitute up to 30% of the tumor mass, are skewed toward an M2-like phenotype by tumor-derived miRNAs, suppressing antigen presentation and promoting secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β, thereby inhibiting T-cell activation ref [30]. Similarly, miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-155 are secreted by glioma cells and taken up by astrocytes and macrophages, inducing reactive phenotypes that further secrete immunosuppressive cytokines and extracellular matrix components conducive to tumor invasion ref [29]. The cross-talk between glioma stem cells and the vascular niche is also modulated by miRNAs, which downregulate chemokines like CXCL10, reducing cytotoxic T-cell infiltration. Additionally, miR-124 and miR-137, often downregulated in glioblastoma, normally promote microglial activation toward an anti-tumor state; their loss contributes to sustained immunosuppression.

Emerging evidence indicates that miRNA-mediated reprogramming extends to endothelial cells and neural precursor cells, which, under tumor influence, adopt pro-tumorigenic functions. For instance, loss of miR-128 in the TME enhances VEGF signaling and vascular permeability, facilitating immune cell exclusion. The combined effect of these miRNA-driven alterations creates a multi-layered barrier to immune surveillance, rendering glioblastoma resistant to immunotherapies even in the presence of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes.

subsections.section_title: miRNA in Immune Evasion and Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Implications of miRNA-Driven Immune Resistance to Checkpoint Inhibitors
subsections.content:
The clinical efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in glioblastoma remains limited, with many patients exhibiting primary or acquired resistance. Emerging evidence implicates miRNA-driven modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment as a key contributor to this resistance. For instance, dysregulated miRNAs can suppress T-cell infiltration and promote an immunosuppressive phenotype by downregulating antigen presentation machinery and enhancing regulatory T-cell activity, thereby blunting the response to anti-PD-1 or anti-CTLA-4 therapies. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that miRNA signatures correlate with poor ICI response, and their expression patterns may serve as predictive biomarkers for patient stratification, as highlighted in studies showing discordance between murine model efficacy and clinical outcomes in glioblastoma ref [33].

Furthermore, exosomal miRNAs secreted by glioblastoma cells can systemically reprogram immune cells in the periphery, inducing tolerance and limiting the systemic activation required for ICI success. This paracrine immune suppression is compounded by the upregulation of alternative immune checkpoints such as IDO and TIM-3, which are themselves regulated by specific miRNAs, as shown in combinatorial blockade studies in murine brain tumor models ref [32]. The failure of monotherapy with ICIs in clinical trials may thus reflect an underlying miRNA-mediated redundancy in immune evasion pathways that cannot be overcome by single-agent blockade ref [31].

Consequently, therapeutic strategies combining ICIs with miRNA-targeting agents—such as antagomiRs or miRNA mimics—hold promise for overcoming resistance. Personalized approaches based on tumor miRNA profiling could enable precision immunotherapy, potentially improving survival in a subset of patients who currently derive minimal benefit from checkpoint blockade.

subsections.section_title: miRNA in Immune Evasion and Tumor Microenvironment
subsections.subsection_title: miRNA Regulation of Immune Checkpoints in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs play a pivotal role in the post-transcriptional regulation of immune checkpoint molecules in glioblastoma, directly influencing tumor immune evasion. Key checkpoints such as PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 are modulated by specific miRNAs that either suppress or enhance their expression, thereby shaping the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. For instance, miR-146a, upregulated in glioblastoma-associated astrocytes, dampens inflammatory signaling by targeting IRAK1 and TRAF6, indirectly promoting an immune-tolerant state that supports PD-L1 expression and T-cell exhaustion ref [4]. Concurrently, global miRNA profiling has identified multiple miRNAs, including miR-200c and miR-138, that directly target PD-L1 mRNA, with their downregulation in glioblastoma correlating with elevated PD-L1 levels and poor clinical outcomes ref [34].

Beyond PD-L1, miRNAs regulate other inhibitory receptors such as BTLA and LAG3, contributing to the multifaceted immune resistance phenotype. The miR-155 family, often overexpressed in glioblastoma, has been shown to suppress SOCS1, leading to enhanced JAK/STAT signaling and subsequent upregulation of multiple immune checkpoint ligands ref [34]. Furthermore, epigenetic silencing of tumor-suppressive miRNAs like miR-137 and miR-124, which normally repress CTLA-4 and PD-1, is frequently observed in glioblastoma stem cells, reinforcing immune evasion mechanisms ref [34]. These findings underscore the centrality of miRNA networks in fine-tuning immune checkpoint expression and highlight their potential as biomarkers or therapeutic targets to restore anti-tumor immunity.

Immunotherapeutic strategies in glioblastoma are increasingly focused on reversing miRNA-mediated immunosuppression, which shapes the tumor microenvironment to evade immune surveillance. Dysregulated miRNAs such as miR-124, miR-155, and miR-21 modulate key immune checkpoints and cytokine networks, directly influencing the function of microglia, macrophages, and dendritic cells. For instance, miR-124 downregulation promotes M2 polarization of tumor-associated macrophages via STAT3 activation, while miR-155 overexpression enhances pro-inflammatory signaling that paradoxically fosters immune tolerance in chronic settings. The network of immunosuppressive pathways in glioblastoma, including TGF-β, IL-10, and CSF-1R signaling, is tightly regulated by miRNA networks, as detailed in comprehensive reviews ref [36]. Targeting these miRNA-regulated axes—such as using antagomiRs against miR-21 to restore PTEN and reduce PD-L1 expression—has shown promise in preclinical models to re-sensitize tumors to immune checkpoint blockade.

Emerging approaches include miRNA-modulated dendritic cell vaccines and CAR-T cells engineered to express miRNA sponges that neutralize immunosuppressive miRNAs within the tumor niche. Notably, IL13Rα2-targeted immunotherapies, while primarily antibody- or cell-based, are now being combined with miRNA modulation to enhance antigen presentation and T-cell infiltration, as highlighted in recent advances ref [37]. Furthermore, miRNA signatures associated with immune evasion, such as those regulating GDF-15 and HIF-1α, are being exploited as biomarkers to stratify patients for immunotherapy ref [36]. The integration of miRNA modulation with immune checkpoint inhibitors, as discussed in broader immunotherapy reviews ref [6], represents a next-generation strategy to overcome the resilience of glioblastoma to single-agent immunotherapies.

subsections.subsection_title: Combination Therapies: miRNA Modulation with Standard Treatments
subsections.content:
Combining miRNA modulation with standard glioblastoma therapies, such as temozolomide (TMZ) and radiotherapy, has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome treatment resistance and enhance therapeutic efficacy. For instance, miR-17 has been shown to sensitize glioblastoma cells to TMZ and low-dose ionizing radiation by regulating autophagy through ATG7 suppression, thereby augmenting cytotoxicity ref [20]. Similarly, silencing miR-21 enhances radiosensitivity by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway and promoting autophagy in malignant glioma cell lines ref [30]. Moreover, let-7b expression modulates chemotherapy response by targeting cyclin D1, suggesting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic adjunct in TMZ regimens ref [17]. Recent clinical evidence supports the synergy of novel physical modalities with standard care: the randomized trial by Stupp et al. demonstrated that tumor-treating fields (TTFields) combined with TMZ significantly improved overall survival compared to TMZ alone, providing a paradigm for integrating non-pharmacological interventions with molecular targeting ref [39].

Further, miR-181c, a tumor suppressor miRNA, attenuates proliferation and invasion in glioblastoma and may potentiate TMZ efficacy by modulating epigenetic regulators ref [37]. Preclinical studies also indicate that restoring miR-137 expression suppresses glioma stem cell stemness and enhances sensitivity to conventional therapies ref [18]. These findings underscore the potential of miRNA-based adjuvants to re-sensitize resistant tumors and extend the therapeutic window of existing standards. Future clinical trials should prioritize biomarker-driven combinations, integrating miRNA profiling with TMZ and TTFields to personalize treatment and improve outcomes in this aggressive malignancy.

subsections.subsection_title: Cell-Based Delivery of miRNAs for Glioblastoma Therapy
subsections.content:
Cell-based delivery systems have emerged as promising strategies for overcoming the blood-brain barrier and achieving targeted miRNA delivery in glioblastoma. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) exhibit intrinsic tropism toward tumor sites and have been successfully engineered to deliver exogenous miRNAs to glioma cells and neural progenitors. In a landmark study, MSCs were shown to transfer miR-124 and miR-145 mimics to co-cultured neural cells, resulting in downregulation of Sox9 and enhanced neuronal differentiation, alongside upregulation of glutamate transporters EAAT1 and EAAT2, thereby mitigating excitotoxicity ref [2]. This paracrine miRNA transfer mechanism avoids the instability and off-target effects associated with synthetic vectors. Beyond MSCs, neural stem cells (NSCs) have also been utilized to deliver tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-128 and miR-34a, suppressing glioma proliferation and stemness in vivo ref [22]. Engineered MSCs expressing miR-146a have demonstrated reduced tumor-associated inflammation by modulating NF-κB signaling, highlighting their dual therapeutic potential ref [20].

Recent advances include the development of miRNA-sensing reporter systems that enable real-time tracking of miRNA delivery efficiency in live cells, enhancing the precision of therapeutic validation ref [2]. Moreover, combining cell-based delivery with biomaterial scaffolds or exosome engineering has improved retention and controlled release at tumor margins. While challenges remain in scalability, immune clearance, and long-term engraftment, cell-based platforms offer a biologically compatible avenue for sustained, localized miRNA modulation in the complex glioblastoma microenvironment.

subsections.subsection_title: miRNA Targeting Strategies: Sponges and Genetic Interference
subsections.content:
MicroRNA sponges represent a powerful genetic interference strategy for achieving sustained, competitive inhibition of specific miRNAs by expressing RNA transcripts with multiple tandem binding sites complementary to the miRNA seed region. This approach effectively sequesters miRNAs from their endogenous mRNA targets, enabling long-term loss-of-function studies in both in vitro and in vivo models. The seminal work by Ebert and Sharp introduced sponges as a versatile tool for probing miRNA function across diverse biological contexts, including cancer, and demonstrated their capacity to inhibit entire miRNA families through seed-region specificity ref [43]. In glioblastoma, lentiviral-mediated expression of a miR-23b sponge significantly reduced tumor malignancy by derepressing key tumor suppressors such as VHL and E-cadherin, while downregulating oncogenic drivers like HIF-1α, MMP2, and VEGF ref [4].

Beyond sponges, genetic interference strategies have expanded to include antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and CRISPR-based systems for precise miRNA knockdown. Notably, targeting miR-10b—a glioblastoma-specific oncogene absent in normal brain tissue—using ASOs delivered via intratumoral, osmotic, or systemic routes effectively suppressed tumor growth in intracranial xenograft models without significant systemic toxicity, highlighting its clinical translatability ref [5]. These approaches offer advantages over transient inhibition methods, enabling durable suppression critical for treating aggressive, recurrent glioblastoma. Recent refinements in sponge design, including optimized binding site spacing and resistance to endogenous RNA degradation, have further enhanced specificity and efficacy, positioning miRNA sponges and genetic interference tools as promising platforms for next-generation RNA therapeutics in neuro-oncology.

The clinical translation of miRNA-based therapeutics for glioblastoma is critically dependent on efficient, targeted delivery systems that overcome the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB). Nanodelivery platforms, particularly liposomal and polymeric nanoparticles, have emerged as promising vehicles for systemic miRNA delivery. Stealth liposomes, such as Caelyx®, demonstrate enhanced intratumoral accumulation in glioblastoma by exploiting the disrupted BBTB, achieving 13–19-fold higher drug concentration in tumors compared to normal brain tissue, thereby improving therapeutic index ref [48]. Beyond liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles made from PLGA and mesoporous silica have been engineered to deliver antisense miR-21 and anti-miR221 PNA, respectively, resulting in significant knockdown of oncogenic miRNAs and synergistic enhancement of temozolomide efficacy in resistant glioma cell lines ref [13], ref [14]. RNA nanoparticles derived from bacteriophage phi29, functionalized with folate ligands, enable specific targeting of glioblastoma cells and effective inhibition of miR-21 in vivo, showcasing the potential of structurally defined RNA nanocarriers ref [12].

Cationic polymers and lipid-based systems further enhance cellular uptake and endosomal escape of miRNA mimics or inhibitors, while surface modifications with peptides or antibodies improve tumor specificity and reduce off-target effects ref [11]. Recent advances in nanoformulations emphasize multi-functional designs that combine miRNA modulation with chemotherapeutics, enabling combinatorial therapy with reduced systemic toxicity ref [49]. The concept of 'whole-process targeting'—adapting nanocarrier properties to dynamic tumor vasculature during progression—offers a strategic framework for optimizing delivery across glioblastoma stages ref [49]. Despite progress, challenges remain in scaling production, ensuring long-term stability, and minimizing immunogenicity. Nevertheless, the convergence of miRNA biology and nanotechnology is paving the way for next-generation therapeutics, with several platforms now advancing toward clinical evaluation.

Figure 1 illustrates the multifaceted roles of microRNAs in glioblastoma pathogenesis, highlighting their involvement in tumor initiation, stemness maintenance, therapy resistance, and immune evasion. Oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-21 and miR-10b are frequently overexpressed and drive proliferation by suppressing key tumor suppressors like PTEN and PDCD4, while tumor-suppressive miRNAs including miR-181c and miR-137 are epigenetically silenced, contributing to unchecked cell growth and self-renewal ref [14], ref [25], ref [50]. MicroRNA dysregulation also modulates the tumor microenvironment; for instance, miR-146a regulates astrocyte-mediated inflammation, and miR-155 influences immune checkpoint dynamics ref [26], ref [30]. Furthermore, miRNAs such as miR-221/222 promote survival by targeting pro-apoptotic factors like PUMA, and miR-17 fine-tunes autophagy to alter temozolomide sensitivity ref [31], ref [27]. The interplay between miRNAs and epigenetic regulators, including EZH2 and KDM5A, establishes a feedback loop that reinforces therapeutic resistance ref [47], ref [45]. These networks are increasingly targeted by novel nanotherapeutics, where nanoparticle-delivered anti-miR oligonucleotides show promise in preclinical models ref [33], ref [41].

The integration of miRNA signatures with genomic and epigenetic profiles enables stratification of glioblastoma subtypes, as demonstrated by genome-wide profiling studies identifying H3F3A and TP53 mutant-specific miRNA patterns ref [15]. Emerging evidence also links exosomal miRNA transfer to intercellular communication within the tumor niche, potentially mediating drug resistance and immune suppression ref [10], ref [26]. Collectively, these findings underscore miRNAs as central nodes in glioblastoma biology and compelling targets for precision therapeutics.

Table 2 summarizes key microRNAs dysregulated in glioblastoma and their validated molecular targets, highlighting their roles in tumor progression, therapy resistance, and stemness maintenance. Notably, miR-128 targets BMI1 and E2F3 to suppress glioma stem cell self-renewal, while miR-34a inhibits NOTCH and MET signaling, thereby reducing tumor invasiveness and promoting differentiation. MiR-184 has been shown to suppress AKT signaling by targeting AKT2, impairing cell survival and proliferation in GBM models. Conversely, oncogenic miR-10b promotes invasion by downregulating HOXD10, and its inhibition reduces tumor dissemination in vivo. MiR-218 acts as a tumor suppressor by targeting SLIT2/ROBO1 and EGFR pathways, with loss correlating with poor prognosis. Additionally, miR-124 and miR-132 regulate neuronal differentiation genes and are frequently silenced in GBM, contributing to de-differentiation. The miR-200 family members, particularly miR-200c, modulate epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers and are downregulated in mesenchymal GBM subtypes, influencing metastatic potential. Finally, miR-326 targets the Notch pathway and the drug efflux pump ABCG2, sensitizing cells to temozolomide and reducing chemoresistance.

Emerging evidence also implicates miR-195 in suppressing CDK6 and CCND1, thereby arresting the cell cycle, and miR-451 in modulating the AMPK/mTOR axis to regulate metabolic adaptation under nutrient stress. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of restoring tumor-suppressive miRNAs or inhibiting oncogenic ones through targeted delivery systems.
